payload.rationale: Neutron's debut has slipped repeatedly: from 2024 to mid-2025, then to late 2025, and in November 2025 Rocket Lab guided to 2026 after Stage 1 qualification and Launch Complex 3 (Wallops) readiness took longer than planned. As of my knowledge, the company continued to target a 2026 first flight, but new orbital vehicles from established and new providers alike (Vulcan, New Glenn, Ariane 6, Starship, Electron itself) almost always miss announced debut windows by many months. With the information cutoff at mid-September 2026 and the contract still apparently open, roughly 3.5 months remain; hitting a first launch in that window requires stage qualification, integrated stage tests, wet dress rehearsals, and static fire to all go smoothly—historically unlikely for a maiden flight. I also allow some probability that the launch already occurred before the cutoff (which would resolve YES) and that Rocket Lab's strong execution culture and pad readiness get a Q4 2026 attempt off. Reasons the estimate may be too high: qualification anomalies (e.g., reported tank test issues), Archimedes engine or stage integration delays, and range/weather constraints in Q4 could easily push the debut into 2027, as has happened with nearly every comparable program. Reasons it may be too low: Rocket Lab has repeatedly stated 2026 as firm, the pad is complete, engine hot-fires were done in 2024–2025, and Beck has strong commercial incentives (NSSL Lane 1, ~$1B+ pipeline) to fly even a risky first attempt before year-end; a launch attempt that lifts off (even if it fails) would likely count as a launch under typical rules.
limitations: No current research supplied; status of Neutron as of September 2026 is unknown to me.
Uncertain whether the launch already occurred before the cutoff.
Contract's precise definition of 'launch' (liftoff vs. success) not provided.
Relies on general base rates for maiden-flight slippage.
